After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Canso public building, $15,000.
Has the site been obtained?

No. The cost of the site will depend altogether on the part of the town in which it is purchased. There have been no negotiations yet for purchasing a site. The populaion is 2,367. The postal revenue is $1,487, and the customs revenue, $1,787.
What is it proposed to spend there ?
It is proposed to spend about $9,500 for the building. Then the heating may cost $1,100, the fittings about $1,500, boxes about $1,700; altogether probably not less than $14,500.
What arrangements are now made for the post, office and custom house ?
They are in a rented Duild-ing. Wo- pay $00 a year for the post office and $50 for the custom house. It is proposed to put up a brick building on a stone foundation.

Well, the minister sees that whilst, with reference to Antigonish, there was a postal revenue amounting to $3,700 and a customs revenue of $7,700, Canso is a town with only $1,487 postal revenue and $1,787 customs revenue, and the minister now proposes to spend, we will say, about $20,000. on a public building in that Mr. HYMAN.
town. The rentals for the two buildings now amount to $110 a year. The other will be running up to $1,200 or $1,300 a year. It does seem as if the minister wTas running the thing pretty well into the ground. You are undertaking to put these expensive public buildings in every part. What do they do in the United States ? That is quite a forward country, with 80,000,000 people, fairly prosperous. What is the principle adopted there with reference to small post offices ?

I must acknowledge that I have not looked closely into the methods pursued in the United States with regard to these matters, and I do not know as we are accustomed to go there for precedents, at least hon. gentlemen opposite tell us we should not. In Canada, when we put up public buildings, we think it is a good principle to make them a credit to the locality and a credit to the country. No doubt by scrimp ing on these buildings we might cut down the expense a little, but I question if, in the long run. that would be in the interests of the country. In making up these estimates I have endeavoured to make the class of buildings fit the localities in which they are erected. In making up these estimates-I desire to be perfectly frank with the committee-I put the sum high enough to cover all probable expenditure, and I expect that we shall be able to keep within the estimate.

What is the trouble with the present arrangements for post office and customs house in Canso ? What is the trouble with the business being carried on under rental as it has been, I suppose, for a number of years ? Did the minister ever think of the system which is in vogue in the United States and other countries, the rental system, not entailing large capital expenditures, where you get a fairly reasonable service for the people ? The minister says it is not always well to look for exsimples on the other side of the line. Just nt this time, when we are building $25,000 post offices in little towns, giving from $1,000 to $3,000 of a revenue, the minister does not want us to go to the United States for an example. I notice the Postmaster General seemed to echo the sentiment of the Minister of Public Works. If the echo were only long enough and persistent enough to reach back eight or ten years, we would hear the hon. gentleman's voice

You can hear it whenever you wish.
Mr. FOSTER-in this chamber very strongly, very vehemently, denouncing the expenditure of large sums of money In small towns for public buildings. I think if the Minister of Public Works would look into the matter as it is carried on in the United States he would find that they have an excellent postal system in small towns and villages, where they use rented buildings. They

give a certain amount as a salary to the postmaster, he finds his place, and finds accommodation, and the people never think of asking the government to erect public buildings in little towns and villages. The Minister of Public Works says he don't want to scrimp. No one asks him to scrimp, but there is such a thing as looking to the source from which the money comes. That source is the hard working men all over this country, many of whom have all they can do to make both ends meet. They have to pay their taxes, and their taxes form a fund into which the hon. gentleman and his colleagues dip. This kind of expenditure is the least valuable that we can make. If you build a railway with public money there is a growing value that returns to the people. They get their goods carried and themselves carried, business is developed, and if you help trade and commerce by subventions, it all tends to growth and development. But a public building in a little town, though it may be nice as a monument, does not bring a revenue, it does not cause any development. It is a nice thing to look upon sometimes, if it is well built, but it does not fructify anything, it does not add anything to the development of the country. You can easily spend a million dollars in that kind of fixed expenditure, but you would much better take the million dollars and put it into what you might call development expenditure. Are we to look upon this as a party measure or as one in the country's interests? If we look upon it in the country's interest, neither of these votes would be in the estimates to-night. But the party is bound to stand by the minister, and to say that the expenditure is good. But the time is coming, our expenditures are increasing so much, that we ought to call a halt upon this method of expenditure. I do not think it is economical; I do not think it is in the interest of the country. What is the rule that the hon. gentleman takes ? If he gives to his friend who represents Guysborough an expensive public building for a small and somewhat thriving fishing town how can he avoid in any fair way of administration giving it to every other town unless he gives simply on the line of distributing it as a part of the party spoils ? My hon. friend may hark back to previous years. Let previous years take care of themselves as far as I am concerned. He can get up and in answer to me he can call up the shades of the past if he pleases, but it is for the present and for the future that we are here and now in the future I am opposed to that kind of expenditure.

If my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) and the House would say that for the future there shall be no expenditure on public buildings, but that in all cases buildings for public purposes shall be rented I have not the least doubt of the possibility of a certain amount of money being saved to the 33
country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster>
takes exception to the erection of these buildings and he says that the time has come to stop expenditures of this kind. The hon. gentleman was in power here for a number of years. He had the honour of being a minister of the Crown and of holding one of the most important positions a* Minister of Finance, and I have just as much right to ask him why the time did not come then when expenditures of this class should be stopped. There is no doubt that this class of expenditure was not inaugurated by this government; it was inaugurated by the previous government, it was carried out by the previous government and if we have erred in this respect it is because we are following in the footsteps of our predecessors in office.
You said it was wrong.
If we said it was wrong you say it is wrong now so that we are on an equal footing.
You promised that if you got in you would remedy it.

If we are to look at this matter simply and solely from the sordid dollars and cents point of view I do not think that expenditures of this character can be completely justified. I am not prepared to say that the time has come when we should simply call a halt and stop entirely the erection of these public buildings. There are a great many counties in which there are no public expenditures of any kind. There are shire towns in which it is only fair and right that we should have a public building without looking at it entirely from the sordid standpoint of dollars and cents. Without any desire to bring up any particular cases in which the old government may have erred in regard to these expenditures, I can only say that in this we are following the precedent which was set up by our predecessors. The hon. gentleman says that these expenditures are entirely political. Let us assume for the moment that the expenditures of the old government were entirely political-and I presume the argument would apply in that case as well as in this -what would be the effect? The effect would be that that party having been ,in power for a number of years they would have public buildings erected in constituencies represented by the party. Is it fair to say that if another party comes into power it shall not erect buildings in the counties which have been overlooked by the previous government? I remember very well that in 1891 a discussion, possibly like the present discussion, took place in which the hon. gentleman who is now the Minister of Public Works very strongly pleaded on behalf of the town of Woodstock. He pointed out that expenditures were being made in very much smaller places, but that no expenditure had ever been made in Wood-



stock although it was a town of 10,000 inhabitants. I think that neglect was afterwards corrected and that an expenditure was made by the hon. gentleman's government. If you look upon these matters purely and simply from the dollars and cents standpoint I do not think that there can be any doubt that the public business can be carried on in a rented building as well as in an office which is built for the purpose. But, that is not entirely the policy of the government. The policy of the government is, when they have public money, when they feel that they can afford to make an expenditure on a public building to erect a public building, to endeavour to keep the amount of the expenditure as low as possible, but to erect a building in accordance with what the Department of Public Works should erect.

I am not going to indulge in anything like the pot calling the kettle black, and I am not going to say the province of Nova Scotia is not entitled to her share of the expenditure, but I would like to see that expenditure devoted to some valuable purpose on the lines set out by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). Take this Canso vote; $800, is four per cent on the money, $S00 additional is the cost of caretaking and maintenance, and $500 is the sinking fund, making $2,100 a year put on the country where $110 now meets everything. I quite agree with what my hon. friend said that this money should be spent efficiently no matter what we haye done In the past. Look at the good that would be accomplished by the establishment of a technical school in a little town like Canso. If we gave $2,000 to every county in Nova Scotia to improve the fisheries, to extend railways, or to be expended in some other progressive way- the people would get a return for the money. But all they get from this expenditure are brick walls to look at. In the erection of a public building there is no advancement in the commercial or educational life of the people. There is a blank brick wall which is practically of no use except that it is an ornament. We are not here to build ornaments, we are here to advance the interests of the people and we are here as the trustees of the people to administer their estate. The money is theirs, it is not ours. The hon. Postmaster General is one whom everybody respects as an administrator of trust funds and I have heard him speak at times very learnedly on that subject. We are here as the administrators of trust funds which are to be administered in the interest of the people who own the money which is not to be squandered. If it has been the practice in the past to justify expenditures of this kind it is high time that practice ceased no matter which party is to blame. Let us administer this money in a way in which it will be profitable and in which it will convey some benefit to the public. I Mr. HYMAN.
would far sooner see this money put into railways, public schools, the promotion of the fisheries or the encouragement of agriculture and things of that kind than see it expended in this way. It would end in the development and progress of the country and the people would learn to appreciate the act of any government that would spend money in that way. I am not taking objection to Nova Scotia getting her share of the money but I do take objection to the doctrine being set up that when good things are going this or that town is to have her share of the good things because some other town had it in the past and that because one party is in power, qow is the time to reward the constituencies friendly to the government. I do not subscribe to those doctrines at all. I repudiate them and I am sorry to hear them enunciated in this House. If the hon. Acting Minister of Public Works would pay a visit to the United States or some other countries and see if there is not some rule that governs in cases of this kind I think the result would prove advantageous to himself and to the country. I have a pretty fair idea of what obtains in the United States. There is a rule-it is not a very strong rule-but there is a general rule that a certain amount will be spent in towns of a certain population and with a certain revenue and in that way those who have these matters in charge can keep a check on the expenditures. But now, we have sent the idea abroad that an expenditure will be made in any town that is friendly to the government-
No.

That is pretty near what we have heard here to-night; that is that any town of 1,500 inhabitants that is friendly to the government can have $25,000 spent on a public building. That is not good policy. There might be a reason for a public building of this kind if we had public ownership of telephones and telegraphs and if the express business were conducted in connection with the post office. But, we have not got that at the present time and that being the ease I say that this expenditure cannot be justified. I oppose it, not because Nova Scotia is not entitled to an expenditure of public money, but because it is not being expended efficiently and it is not our duty as trustees to squander the public money as it has been squandered in these votes.

I entertain the same opinion to-day in regard to expenditures on buildings of this character as that which I have entertained for many years, and I hold that no government has any business to expend money on that principle. We have post offices all over the country and have a somewhat extensive experience as to the cost. Take towns and villages with the

same population and the same amount of *business,, and you will find that in every instance where we rent the building it costs the country very much less, in most cases not one-fourth of the money that it costs to erect our own buildings. Then we put up buildings in some small places while in large towns never a dollar has been spent for public buildings, and to-day we have only rented buildings in them. Take, if you like, the county of Grey, which 1 represent. It is one of the largest counties in Ontario, with a population of about 75,000. If you take Meaford in that county with a revenue of $3,807, which shows that it is a live, prosperous town, yon will find that not a dollar has been spent for a post office, but people there have not clamoured for the expenditure because there is a good postoffice building built by a private individual and all we pay for that is $160 a year as an allowance for rent, fuel and light. $160 a year covers all the expense of a building for a place which is as large or larger than Antigonish or the place where we now propose to put up a post office. What justification can there be for incurring an annual outlay of over $1,200 a year to give the same accommodation to the public which they can receive for $160. It is a very bad business principle. Then take Owen Sound, one of the best towns in Ontario, a town of 10,000 population, but up to the present there has not been a dollar spent for a post office. They have a building rented there at a very much less cost than the interest in the investment and the cost of caring for a government building. Not many years ago when the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) was running up there the Postmaster General visited that town and picked out a very nice site-

I never did anything of the kind.

I am speaking of Owen Sound.

What I have said in Owen Sound is : Owen Sound has magnificent harbour facilities and I think that Owen Sound requires the improvement of its harbour to enable it to make money. That would be better for Owen Sound than to spend money on public buildings that otherwise might very properly be erected. I took this argument and I leave it to my hon. friend if that is not correct. No matter what must be the claims, no matter how justifiable it would be to expend for post office building and harbour works, after all there is a limit to what the country will pay to any particular place, and I have pointed out to the people, not of Owen Sound alone, but of other places, when they have discussed with me from time to time proposed expenditures to public buildings, I have asked them : is there not some other way, is there not something more urgent that would be a more useful expenditure than would the erection of public buildings? My recommendation to them is to see that the application is first made in regard to public works that are of greater urgency and likely to be more advantageous. I have given that advice constantly to people from places like Owen Sound. I did so in Meaford ; my hon. friend refers to Meaford. It is not many weeks since some gentlemen from Meaford proposed to me, thinking I had something to do with the recommendations for the building of post offices, that I should, in the interest of M.eaford, recommend the appropriation of some money for a public building. We have commenced to develop Meaford harbour and my hon. friend will justify, I am sure, all we have done there.
Yes.

And will justify more. It has a bright future if wo enable it to trade outside. That is the kind of argument I have advanced at Meaford and at other places. There are some places

not so situated geographically where wharfs, &c., can he of service, inland towns or places that are not in need of harbour facilities; these places may press for expenditure on public buildings, but we have had to contend with the effect of a bad example. The public have been falsely educated. For example, I have before me a paper and 1 will show you-but I did not intend to cut in on the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and I must apologize. I will later on show where we have been left by the bad example I spoke of.
What did you go upstairs for ?

I only hope the Postmaster General will be fortified with sufficient strength to withstand this bad example and adopt better principles. I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) to what a splendid rebuke this is to his policy in regard to post offices, and the principle is a good one, if they only lived up to it. I will say with regard to the Postmaster General that he must have been very unfortunate in the choice of his language in explaining the situation in Owen Sound, for my information was that he went down and showed what a splendid place they had for a dry dock, how much they required for harbours, how badly they needed a post office, and what a fine thing it would be to have all their workmen employed. I had been speaking there and I said that no matter what candidate was returned the government would have to do justice, and then along came Mr. Hardy and said : Oh yes, you will get justice, but there is a difference between cold justice and hot justice. Hot justice was an active commerce, employment for the labourers, expenditure of money in the town, fine buildings going up, improvements to the harbour, and expansion of commerce. This was the warm justice they were going to get in contradistinction to the cold justice which would be meted out if they sent an opponent of the government. The Postmaster General being there two different parties were vying with each other in the effort to sell a site and one of them, who had always been a Conservative, told me in the hotel that but for the fact that he had reasonable hopes of being able to sell a site to the Postmaster General he would support our candidate, but he said : You know I am hard up and anxious to sell my lot, therefore I cannot afford to oppose them. He was unfortunate in his language, because that is the impression he left.

The hon. gentleman has no information except hearsay. Mr. Hopkins he says, told him. I never knew a member of this House more given to founding statements on hearsay than the hon. member. He begins a statement by

saying ' I have heard,' ' rumour says,' ' a man told me,' &c. He is a regular Sarey Gamp with a ridiculous Mrs. Harris. I ask the hon. gentleman to desist from charging me with doing a thing when I did not do it.

I think it is quite gratuitous to intimate that I am in the habit of basing statements on hearsay. I have given the name of a respectable gentleman in Owen Sound who has been there for 30 years or more.

He walked in in my presence along with the Postmaster General. I happened to be in the hotel because I was staying there. Is that not good evidence ?

I submit it is. Let the Postmaster General go Into Owen Sound and say that the evidence of Hopkins is not reliable. I can tell him one thing, that he would not get a very courteous reply. If; the Owen Sound ' Advertiser,' which supports the hon. gentleman, does not bear out in the main what I say with regard to the impressions left on the people's mind, 1 will admit that I was entirely wrong in my impression. But I believe I was justified in every particular. With regard to Mea-ford, I said nothing. About the wisdom of spending money on harbours instead of post offices, I agree with the hon. Postmaster General. The expenditure on Meaford harbour was an admirable expenditure and served a good purpose. If the hon. gentleman proposed to-morrow to spend money for a post office in Meaford, I do not know that I would justify it. Meaford has now a good post office^ which costs the country only $160 a year* whereas, it would be impossible to have a good building put up there at a less cost than double or treble that amount. places, because the public are now provide^ with accommodation for less cost than they! would be if the buildings were put. up. When the Post-i master General and his friends were on this side of the House. I took the same ground. I said, as a supporter of the government at that time, that whenever the government could not get a suitable building for a moderate figure, they might be justified in erecting a building, but otherwise they would not.

The main argument used by some of the hon. gentlemen who have addressed the committee is that we should rent buildings for custom houses or post offices. I wish to point out that in Canso we are absolutely without decent facilities at the present time. The occasion of applying for this building was a fire, in which the existing custom house was burned. The business is now carried on in a dwelling house, a very inconvenient place. There is no building in the town at all suitable that could be secured by the government. The post office is in a small wooden building, something like 8 by 10 feet. It is so'small that the people have to stand outside in the snow on stormy nights while the mail is being sorted, and there is no place to shelter them while the mail is being delivered. This small building was erected by the postmaster because there was no other suitable building. I may also point out that while the revenue from the custom house is small, a large business is carried on in connection with it. Canso is the principal fishing station on the eastern coast of Nova Scotia.
It is now the headquarters of the banking fleet, and a large number of vessels call there year after year. I find on looking at the trade and navigation returns that thu 'lumber of vessels engaged in the coasting trade which called at Canso last year was 802, with a tonnage of 41.349 tons, and having crews numbering 4,988 ; the number of steamers was 607, with a tonnage of 63,317 tons, and crews numbering 6,249 ; the number of vessels outward bound for sea was 466, with a tonnage of 41,066 and crews numbering 6,909 ; making altogether 1,875 vessels calling at that port during the last year, with a tonnage of 145,732 tons, and crew's numbering 18,227 men ; showing the committee that there is a large business done in the custom house there, although the revenue is small.
How does the hon. gentleman account for that ?
It is the duty of the customs officer to enter these ships and report them.
These are fishing vessels.

Fishing vessels, from which there is no revenue at all. Canso is not an importing point. A large quantity of goods are used there, but they are imported chiefly from Halifax. Consequently, the amount of duties paid there is small, but the officer has a great deal of work, which he is required to do under the Merchants 'Shipping Act. Canso is a growing town. Some complaint was made in connection with the last item that we were voting money for a town that was decreasing in population. By the census, I find that the popluation of Canso in 4871 was 1,090, in 1881 1,411, in 1891, 1,824, and in 1901, 2,367, an increase of 35 per cent during the last ten years. The number of money orders issued there last year was 2,583, and the amount of money transmitted $29,750.98. Besides being the headquarters of the fishing industry in Nova Scotia, Canso is a cable station. Eight or ten cables are landed there, it has two large stations, one under the management of the Western Union, the other under the management of the Commercial Cable Company. The committee will therefore see that it is absolutely necessary to provide this accommodation at Canso, owing to the fact that there is no building that could be rented at the preseit time.

Yes.

If the government have not a building of that kind already, this ought to be erected without question, for, we are getting into this country a class of immigrants absolutely inferior to the class allowed to enter the United States. No matter what is said, as a matter of fact, they are coming in, and from here they are filtering into the United States. No time should be lost in providing the proper housing to care for and examining these men. If they are not all right, send them back. We are getting a lot of people who have no right to come here, especially men from southern Italy, who have contagious diseases. If the government has not proper quarantine build-1 ings in St. John, Halifax and Quebec to look

after these people, the money should not require to be re-voted, but should be spent at once.

In Quebec they have a building for this purpose, erected, I think, last year. In the present estimates. I think, will be found a vote for a similar building in Halifax. This one is for St. John, and, as I have explained Dr. Bryce is there at the present time to choose the site. I have instructed the chief architect to call Dr. Bryce's attention to the matter immediately on his return, and we shall endeavour to proceed with the building at once.

Dr. Bryce was there last summer in plenty of time to have the building started. It is evidently intended not to make it an expensive building. If they have not the site, they know about where it is to go. There has been no delay, as far as I can gather, on the part of Dr. Bryce, but the delay appears to be on the part of the government. As the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has stated, this is a building that is very much needed for the purpose of detaining the people who are physically unfit to be allowed to go loose in the country

people suffering from trachoma, favus and other contagious diseases. Such a building is now urgently needed. All this winter immigrants have been coming in through St. John ; and certainly we have heard no good reason why, when the money was voted last-year, the work has not been carried out.
